Chapter 6: Navigating Cognitive Biases—Seeing Others, and Ourselves, More Clearly.
As we move further along this journey, something becomes pretty obvious: understanding other people isn’t just about reading them. It’s also about recognizing the mental filters we use—those little shortcuts our brains take, called cognitive biases. They help us make quick sense of things, but honestly, they can really twist how we see someone’s emotions or intentions.
Let’s talk about a few of the most common biases you might run into when you’re trying to read people.
First up, there’s confirmation bias. Ever found yourself just noticing things that back up what you already believe about someone, while you kind of ignore the rest? Let’s say you think a coworker is unfriendly. Suddenly, every curt email stands out, but those rare moments when they’re actually warm? You might just miss them.
Then there’s attribution error. This one’s sneaky. We tend to explain other people’s actions by blaming their character—like, “She’s careless”—instead of considering what might be happening in their day. Maybe she’s just overwhelmed right now. When we jump to conclusions, we not only risk being unfair, but we also miss a chance to show a little empathy.
And let’s not forget about projection. Sometimes, without even realizing it, we put our own feelings or motives onto someone else. We assume they’re thinking or feeling just like us, even when they’re not.
So, how do you counteract these biases? Here are a few practical steps you can try.
First, pause and reflect. The next time you feel a strong reaction to what someone does, ask yourself, “What else could explain this?” That one question can open up a whole new way of seeing the situation.
Second, look for evidence that goes against your assumptions. If you think someone’s checked out, pay attention to those times when they’re actually engaged or interested. You might be surprised by what you find.
And finally, check in with others. Sometimes, a friend or a trusted colleague can see things from a totally different angle, and that fresh perspective can help you get past your own filters.
Let’s put this into a real-life context. Picture a team that thinks their manager doesn’t care. They take a step back and consider how much that manager actually has on their plate. Maybe they even ask around. Suddenly, it becomes clear—the manager isn’t disinterested. They’re just overwhelmed. That one shift in perspective can lead to so much more compassion and better teamwork.
Here’s the key takeaway: noticing and managing our own cognitive biases is like cleaning the lens we use to look at others. It’s not a one-and-done thing—it takes humility and self-awareness, and it’s something we have to keep working on. But if you want to truly understand people, it’s absolutely essential.
